rationale: Matthew tells of two blind men twice, and the two scenes share checkable wording. A case-insensitive, word-boundary script over this app's BSB finds "two blind men" only at 9:27 and 20:30 in the whole Bible, "have mercy on us" in Matthew only at 9:27, 20:30 and 20:31, and "touched their eyes" only at 9:29 and 20:34. Both pairs call Jesus "Son of David," and in both scenes their eyes are opened (9:30; 20:33). In Greek the touch is not worded identically in every edition: 9:29 reads ophthalmon ("eyes") in all editions Bible Hub lists, while 20:34 reads ommaton in the Nestle 1904, Westcott-Hort, SBL and Tischendorf editions and ophthalmon in the Byzantine, Greek Orthodox and Textus Receptus editions. Motif/strong, following conn-matt17-passion-matt16 (a recurrence within one Gospel): the repetition is close and checkable. The differences are as clear. At 9:27-31 the men follow Jesus into a house, are asked about faith, and are sternly told to keep silent. At 20:29-34 they sit by the road outside Jericho, the crowd tries to silence them, and Jesus acts "Moved with compassion." Whether the two scenes are one event told twice is disputed: Ulrich Luz reads a duplication by Matthew, and R. T. France reads two separate traditions (both as quoted by Christian Think Tank, secondhand). The grade covers the repeated wording only.
